notes.meaning: Eliphaz is the first of Job's three friends to reply. He was probably the oldest and most respected member of the group, and he came from Teman, a place known for its wise men. He waited respectfully in silence for a whole week, but he now feels compelled to answer Job's bitter lament.

Eliphaz begins with polite hesitation, asking if Job can bear to hear a word of counsel. Even so, he explains that he and his friends cannot keep quiet after hearing Job complain against God's providence.

Eliphaz reminds Job of his long habit of comforting other people in their trials. Job had often strengthened drooping hands, steadied shaking knees, and counseled those who were stumbling under their burdens.

Now that deep suffering has struck Job himself, he is overwhelmed and loses heart. Eliphaz faults him for collapsing under trouble instead of practicing the very patience and faith he once urged upon others.

Eliphaz asks whether Job's past reverence toward God and his upright life should not give him confidence and hope. If his faith was genuine, he ought to trust God for deliverance rather than sinking into despair.

Eliphaz asks Job to think back over history and name a single innocent person who was ever destroyed by God. He assumes that God never abandons the righteous to ruin, which secretly hints that Job's disasters must be the result of hidden sin.

Eliphaz points to his own observations in life, comparing human behavior to farming. People who deliberately plow the ground for evil and plant trouble will inevitably harvest suffering as their reward.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some prosperity teachers treat sowing and reaping as a strict law in this life, arguing that suffering or sickness always proves a person planted sin or lacked faith.

notes.meaning: God does not need great weapons to bring down evil people, because a single blast of His anger can sweep them away like chaff. Eliphaz sees destructive storms and sudden disasters as direct displays of God's wrath against sin.

Eliphaz compares cruel, powerful oppressors to fierce lions that hunt down their prey. Even the strongest predators have their teeth broken by God, eventually starving to death while their young are scattered without help.
Eliphaz claims divine authority for his words by describing a revelation given to him in secret. The message came softly and quietly, and his ears caught only a faint whisper of its full mystery.

This message arrived in a vision during the night, when deep sleep had fallen on the people around him. In the days before the Bible was written down, God often communicated His will through visions in the quiet hours of darkness.
The encounter filled Eliphaz with dread, making his whole body shake and his bones tremble. Human beings naturally feel terror and weakness whenever they are confronted with a supernatural presence.
A mysterious spiritual presence glided past Eliphaz's face in the dark. The sight was so chilling that the hair on his skin stood up on end.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe this spirit was a demon rather than a holy messenger, arguing that it brought dark fear and hid in shadows rather than bringing godly comfort.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars translate the word as a rush of wind rather than an apparition, noting that wind often signals God's powerful presence.

notes.meaning: The figure stopped and stood before him, yet its outline remained dim and indistinct. After an eerie silence settled over the room, a gentle, quiet voice spoke out of the stillness.

The voice asked whether any mortal human can be more righteous or pure than God the Maker. Since God is perfectly just, frail people have no right to question His actions or complain that He treats them unfairly.

Even heavenly messengers are merely creatures who fall infinitely short of God's perfect holiness. If God sees limitations in His angels, no earthly human can ever claim to be completely blameless in His sight.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition often sees this verse as a reference to the fall of the angels who rebelled against God before humanity was created.

notes.meaning: Human beings are far more frail than angels, living in mortal bodies made from the dust like houses of clay. People are so delicate and short-lived that they can be crushed as easily as a moth.
Human life is so fragile that people can be broken and ruined between morning and evening. Men and women pass away continually, dying out of this world without most people even noticing.

Death pulls up the cords of life just as a person collapses a traveler's tent, stripping away all earthly wealth and strength. Many people die without ever learning the true wisdom that life and suffering were meant to teach them.
